claim: The clinical and societal measurement of human sleep has increased exponentially in recent years.
source: The clinical and societal measurement of human sleep has increased exponentially in recent years.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript itself, though it reflects a trend discussed in the introduction.

claim: Basic and clinical sleep research still relies on human visual scoring.
source: However, unlike other fields of medical analysis that have become highly automated, basic and clinical sleep research still relies on human visual scoring.
evidence: This statement is supported by discussion in the introduction about current practices and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Human-based sleep evaluations are time-consuming, tedious, and can be prone to subjective bias.
source: Such human-based evaluations are time-consuming, tedious, and can be prone to subjective bias.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction discussing interscorer variability and time requirements.

claim: The algorithm was trained and validated on +30,000 hr of polysomnographic sleep recordings across heterogeneous populations around the world.
source: Here, we describe a novel algorithm trained and validated on +30,000 hr of polysomnographic sleep recordings across heterogeneous populations around the world.
evidence: This is directly supported by the descriptive statistics section which details the training set composition.

claim: The tool offers high sleep-staging accuracy that matches human scoring accuracy and interscorer agreement no matter the population kind.
source: This tool offers high sleep-staging accuracy that matches human scoring accuracy and interscorer agreement no matter the population kind.
evidence: This is supported by the validation results showing comparable performance to human scorers across different populations.

claim: Adequate sleep supports immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems.
source: Adequate sleep supports a panoply of physiological body functions, including immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems (Besedovsky et al., 2019; Cappuccio and Miller, 2017; Harding et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by three citations to published research.

claim: Sufficient sleep facilitates optimal learning, memory, attention, mood, and decision-making processes.
source: Within the brain, sufficient sleep facilitates optimal learning, memory, attention, mood, and decision-making processes (Ben Simon et al., 2020; Walker, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by two citations to published research.

claim: Improving sleep health has emerged as a preventive strategy to reduce the risk of cardiovascular and metabolic disease, all-cause mortality risk, and the accumulation of Alzheimer's disease pathology within the brain.
source: Improving sleep health has therefore emerged as a preventive strategy to reduce the risk of cardiovascular and metabolic disease, all-cause mortality risk, and more recently, the accumulation of Alzheimer's disease pathology within the brain (Cappuccio et al., 2010; Leary et al., 2020Cappuccio and Miller, 2017; Ju et al., 2014; Winer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The demand for quantifying human sleep at a research-, clinical-, and consumer-based level has increased expeditiously over the past decade.
source: Considering this impact, the demand for quantifying human sleep at a research-, clinical-, and consumer-based level has increased expeditiously over the past decade (Fleming et al., 2015; Shelgikar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by two citations to published research.

claim: Polysomnography is the gold standard for objective physiological quantification of human sleep.
source: Polysomnography (PSG) – the simultaneous measurement of brainwaves, eye movements, muscle activity, heart rate, and respiration – is the gold standard for objective physiological quantification of human sleep.
evidence: This is a widely accepted fact in sleep medicine and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Sleep scoring is typically performed by humans by dividing the night of PSG recording into 30 s segments called 'epochs'.
source: Currently, such sleep scoring is typically performed by humans, accomplished by first dividing the night of PSG recording into 30 s segments (called 'epochs').
evidence: This is consistent with standard AASM guidelines referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Each epoch is assigned a sleep stage based on standard rules defined by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
source: Each epoch is then assigned a sleep stage based on standard rules defined by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM, Berry et al., 2012; Iber et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to AASM guidelines.

claim: Visual scoring of a single night of human sleep requires up to 2 hr to complete by a well-trained individual.
source: It is a non-trivial, time-intensive process, with visual scoring of a single night of human sleep requiring up to 2 hr to complete by a well-trained individual.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the time requirements of manual sleep scoring.

claim: Human sleep scoring has approximately 83% interscorer consistency of agreement.
source: As if not more critical, this human-scored approach suffers from issues of lower than desirable interscorer consistency of agreement (~83% agreement, Rosenberg and Van Hout, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The same scoring individual typically experiences approximately 90% intrascorer agreement of the same sleep recording.
source: Moreover, the same scoring individual typically experiences low intrascorer agreement of the same sleep recording (~90%, Fiorillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Sun et al., 2017 reported an algorithm trained and evaluated on 2000 PSG recordings from a single-sleep clinic with an overall Cohen's kappa of 0.68 on the testing set.
source: Sun et al., 2017 reported an algorithm that was trained and evaluated on 2000 PSG recordings from a single-sleep clinic. The overall Cohen's kappa on the testing set was 0.68 (n = 1000 PSG nights).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The Z3Score algorithm was trained and evaluated on ~1700 PSG recordings from four datasets with overall accuracy ranging from 89.8% in healthy adults/adolescents to 72.1% in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: Thereafter, and algorithm termed 'Z3Score' (Patanaik et al., 2018) was published, trained and evaluated on ~1700 PSG recordings from four datasets. Here, the overall accuracy ranged from 89.8% in healthy adults/adolescents to 72.1% in patients with Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The Stanford-stage algorithm was trained and evaluated on 10 clinical cohorts (~3000 recordings) with an accuracy of 87% against consensus human sleep stage scoring.
source: The freely available 'Stanford-stage' algorithm (Stephansen et al., 2018) was trained and evaluated on 10 clinical cohorts (~3000 recordings), and presented with an accuracy of 87% against consensus human sleep stage scoring.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The SeqSleepNet algorithm was trained and tested using a 20-fold cross-validation of 200 nights of PSG data with an overall accuracy of 87.1%.
source: A year later, the 'SeqSleepNet' algorithm (Phan et al., 2019) was published, which represented a method trained and tested using a 20-fold cross-validation of 200 nights of PSG data, with an overall accuracy of 87.1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The U-Sleep algorithm was established using PSG recordings from 15,660 participants of 16 clinical studies with a mean F1-score of 0.79 for healthy adults and 0.76 for patients with sleep apnea.
source: Finally, the recent U-Sleep algorithm (Perslev et al., 2021) was established using PSG recordings from 15,660 participants of 16 clinical studies. The overall accuracy was not reported, though the mean F1-score—a measure reflecting the quality of the prediction against the consensus scoring of five human experts—was 0.79 for healthy adults and 0.76 for patients with sleep apnea.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The training set consisted of more than 31,000 hr of PSG data across 3163 unique full-night PSG recordings from seven different datasets.
source: The training set consisted of more than 31,000 hr of PSG data across 3163 unique full-night PSG recordings from seven different datasets (Cleveland Children's Sleep and Health Study [CCSHS], n = 414; Cleveland Family Study [CFS], n = 586; Childhood Adenotonsillectomy Trial [CHAT], n = 351; Home Positive Airway Pressure [HomePAP], n = 82; Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis [MESA], n = 575; Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study [MrOS], n = 565; Sleep Heart Health Study [SHHS], n = 590).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The 3163 training nights represent almost 4 million unique 30 s epochs.
source: In total, these 3163 training nights represent almost 4 million unique 30 s epochs.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the training data described.

claim: The average apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) in the training set was 12.9 ± 16.35 with a median of 6.95 and range of 0–125.
source: The average apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 12.9 ± 16.35 (median = 6.95, range = 0–125).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The AHI was ≥15 (moderate sleep apnea) for 29% of the nights in the training set.
source: The AHI was ≥15 (= moderate sleep apnea) for 29% of the nights.
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The MESA dataset had the highest average AHI (19.2 ± 18.1) in the training set.
source: The MESA dataset had the highest average AHI (19.2 ± 18.1), while the CCSHS had the lowest AHI (1.5 ± 5.2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The CCSHS dataset had the lowest AHI (1.5 ± 5.2) in the training set.
source: The MESA dataset had the highest average AHI (19.2 ± 18.1), while the CCSHS had the lowest AHI (1.5 ± 5.2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The testing set 1 consisted of 585 unique full-night PSG recordings from six different datasets.
source: The testing set 1 consisted of 585 unique full-night PSG recordings from six different datasets (CCSHS, n = 100; CFS, n = 99; CHAT, n = 100; MESA, n = 97; MrOS, n = 90; SHHS, n = 99).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The 585 testing nights represent 716,367 unique 30 s epochs, or roughly 6000 hr of PSG data.
source: In total, these 585 testing nights represent 716,367 unique 30 s epochs, or roughly 6000 hr of PSG data.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the testing data described.

claim: There was no significant difference in the sex ratio, race distribution, or in the proportion of individuals diagnosed with insomnia, depression, or diabetes between training and testing set 1.
source: Importantly, there was no significant difference in the sex ratio, race distribution, or in the proportion of individuals diagnosed with insomnia, depression, or diabetes.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparisons presented in Table 1.

claim: Age and body mass index (BMI) were lower in the testing set compared to the original training set (p's<0.05), although the effect sizes of these differences were all below 0.17.
source: Although participants were randomly assigned in the training/testing sets, there were some significant differences between these two sets. Specifically, age and body mass index (BMI) were lower in the testing set compared to the original training set (p's<0.05), although the effect sizes of these differences were all below 0.17 (considered small or negligible).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparisons presented in Table 1.

claim: The testing set 2 consisted of 80 full-night PSG recordings from the publicly available Dreem Open Dataset (DOD) dataset.
source: The testing set 2 consisted of 80 full-night PSG recordings from the publicly available Dreem Open Dataset (DOD) dataset (Guillot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: The DOD consists of 25 nights from healthy adults (DOD-Healthy: age = 35.3 ± 7.51 years, 76% male, BMI = 23.8 ± 3.4).
source: The DOD consists of 25 nights from healthy adults (DOD-Healthy: age = 35.3 ± 7.51 years, 76% male, BMI = 23.8 ± 3.4) and 55 nights from patients with OSA (DOD-Obstructive: age = 45.6 ± 16.5 years, 64% male, BMI = 29.6 ± 6.4, AHI = 18.5 ± 16.2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section, with citation to the source.

claim: The DOD consists of 55 nights from patients with OSA (DOD-Obstructive: age = 45.6 ± 16.5 years, 64% male, BMI = 29.6 ± 6.4, AHI = 18.5 ± 16.2).
source: The DOD consists of 25 nights from healthy adults (DOD-Healthy: age = 35.3 ± 7.51 years, 76% male, BMI = 23.8 ± 3.4) and 55 nights from patients with OSA (DOD-Obstructive: age = 45.6 ± 16.5 years, 64% male, BMI = 29.6 ± 6.4, AHI = 18.5 ± 16.2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section, with citation to the source.

claim: Five nights were excluded from the DOD because the duration of the PSG data and the duration of the hypnogram differed by more than 1 min, leading to a final sample of 75 nights.
source: Five nights were excluded because the duration of the PSG data and the duration of the hypnogram differed by more than 1 min, leading to a final sample of 75 nights (~607 hr of data).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: Each night of the testing set 2 was scored by five registered sleep technicians.
source: Each night of the testing set 2 was scored by five registered sleep technicians, thus allowing to test the algorithm against a consensus of human scorers (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is directly stated in the descriptive statistics section.

claim: Median accuracy of the algorithm on testing set 1 was 87.46%.
source: Median accuracy, calculated across all 585 testing nights, was 87.46%.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The median Cohen's kappa on testing set 1 was 0.819, indicating excellent agreement.
source: The median Cohen's kappa was 0.819, indicating excellent agreement, and similarly, the median Matthews correlation coefficient was 0.821.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The median Matthews correlation coefficient on testing set 1 was 0.821.
source: The median Cohen's kappa was 0.819, indicating excellent agreement, and similarly, the median Matthews correlation coefficient was 0.821.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The CCSHS database testing set had the highest overall accuracy (median = 90.44%).
source: The CCSHS database testing set had the highest overall accuracy (median = 90.44%), while the MESA database had the lowest accuracy (median = 83.99%).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MESA database had the lowest accuracy (median = 83.99%) in testing set 1.
source: The CCSHS database testing set had the highest overall accuracy (median = 90.44%), while the MESA database had the lowest accuracy (median = 83.99%).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median confidence of the algorithm across all the testing nights was 85.79%.
source: The median confidence of the algorithm across all the testing nights was 85.79%.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: Nights with a higher average confidence had significantly higher accuracy (r = 0.76, p<0.001).
source: Nights with a higher average confidence had significantly higher accuracy (Figure 1B, r = 0.76, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The overall sensitivity of N3 sleep was 83.2%, leading to a median F1-score across all testing nights of 0.835.
source: The overall sensitivity (i.e., the percent of epochs that were correctly classified, see Materials and methods) of N3 sleep was 83.2%, leading to a median F1-score across all testing nights of 0.835.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: REM sleep, N2 sleep, and wakefulness all showed sensitivities above 85% (all median F1-scores ≥ 0.86).
source: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, N2 sleep, and wakefulness all showed sensitivities above 85% (all median F1-scores ≥ 0.86).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: N1 sleep showed the lowest agreement, with an overall sensitivity of 45.4% and a median F1-score of 0.432.
source: N1 sleep showed the lowest agreement, with an overall sensitivity of 45.4% and a median F1-score of 0.432 – a finding consistent with this sleep stage often showing very low agreement across human sleep scorers (<45%, Malhotra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1C, with citation to support the comparison to human scorers.

claim: N1 sleep often shows very low agreement across human sleep scorers (<45%).
source: N1 sleep showed the lowest agreement, with an overall sensitivity of 45.4% and a median F1-score of 0.432 – a finding consistent with this sleep stage often showing very low agreement across human sleep scorers (<45%, Malhotra et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The two most common inaccuracies of the algorithm were mislabeling N1 sleep as N2 sleep (27.5% of all true N1 sleep epochs) and mislabeling N3 sleep as N2 sleep (16.1% of all true N3 sleep epochs).
source: Further examination of the confusion matrix showed that the two most common inaccuracies of the algorithm were (1) mislabeling N1 sleep as N2 sleep (27.5% of all true N1 sleep epochs) and (2) mislabeling N3 sleep as N2 sleep (16.1% of all true N3 sleep epochs).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The algorithm made few blatant errors, such as mislabeling N3 sleep as REM sleep (0.2%) or mislabeling REM sleep as N3 sleep (0.03%).
source: Importantly, the algorithm made few blatant errors, such as mislabeling N3 sleep as REM sleep (0.2%) or mislabeling REM sleep as N3 sleep (0.03%).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When the algorithm misclassified an epoch, the second highest probability stage predicted by the algorithm was the correct one in 76.3% ± 12.6% of the time.
source: In addition, when the algorithm misclassified an epoch, the second highest probability stage predicted by the algorithm was the correct one in 76.3% ± 12.6% of the time.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The algorithm was more prone to inaccuracies around sleep-stage transitions than during stable epochs (mean accuracy around a stage transition: 69.15% ± 7.23%, during stable periods: 94.08% ± 5.61%, p<0.001).
source: Additional analyses indicated that the algorithm was more prone to inaccuracies around sleep-stage transitions than during stable epochs (Figure 2F; mean accuracy around a stage transition: 69.15% ± 7.23%, during stable periods: 94.08% ± 5.61%, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Accuracy was significantly greater for epochs flagged by the algorithm as high confidence (≥80% confidence) than in epochs with a confidence below 80% (95.90% ± 3.70% and 62.91% ± 6.6%, respectively, p<0.001).
source: Similarly, and as expected, accuracy was significantly greater for epochs flagged by the algorithm as high confidence (≥80% confidence) than in epochs with a confidence below 80% (95.90% ± 3.70% and 62.91% ± 6.6%, respectively, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The algorithm was most confident in epochs scored as wakefulness by the human scorer (mean confidence across all epochs = 92.7%).
source: The algorithm was most confident in epochs scored as wakefulness by the human scorer (mean confidence across all epochs = 92.7%) and least confident in epochs scored as N1 sleep (mean = 63.2%).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The algorithm was least confident in epochs scored as N1 sleep (mean = 63.2%).
source: The algorithm was most confident in epochs scored as wakefulness by the human scorer (mean confidence across all epochs = 92.7%) and least confident in epochs scored as N1 sleep (mean = 63.2%).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The overall proportion of each sleep stage in the testing nights was similar between the human and automatic staging (all Cohen's d < 0.11).
source: The overall proportion of each sleep stage in the testing nights was similar between the human and automatic staging (all Cohen's d < 0.11; Figure 1D), indicating a negligible bias.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The percentage of stage transitions across the night was consistent in the human and automatic scoring (mean ± STD: 11.12% ± 5.19% and 11.46% ± 4.11%, respectively, Cohen's d = 0.07).
source: Similarly, the percentage of stage transitions across the night was consistent in the human and automatic scoring (mean ± STD: 11.12% ± 5.19% and 11.46% ± 4.11%, respectively, Cohen's d = 0.07).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The median accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring of the five experts on DOD-Healthy was 86.6%.
source: In healthy adults, the median accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring of the five experts was 86.6%.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: The median kappa across all nights on DOD-Healthy was 80.1%, indicating excellent agreement.
source: The median kappa across all nights was 80.1%, indicating excellent agreement.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The accuracy of YASA on the DOD-Healthy dataset was not significantly different from the two other deep-learning-based sleep-staging algorithms or any of the individual scorers (except scorer 4).
source: Pairwise t-tests adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm method revealed that the accuracy of YASA on this healthy validation dataset was not significantly different from the two other deep-learning-based sleep-staging algorithms or any of the individual scorers (except scorer 4, see below or Table 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: Scorer 4 had a significantly lower F1-score for N1 (p=0.034) and N2 (p<0.001) on DOD-Healthy, resulting in a lower overall accuracy (p=0.001).
source: Scorer 4 had a significantly lower F1-score for N1 (p=0.034) and N2 (p<0.001), resulting in a lower overall accuracy (p=0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: The Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm had significantly higher F1-scores than YASA for N1, REM sleep and wakefulness on DOD-Healthy (p=0.006, p<0.001, and p=0.042, respectively).
source: The Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm had significantly higher F1-scores than YASA for N1, REM sleep and wakefulness (p=0.006, p<0.001, and p=0.042, respectively).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: F1-scores for N2 and N3 were not statistically different between YASA and the Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm on DOD-Healthy.
source: F1-scores for N2 and N3 were not statistically different between YASA and the Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: The median accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring of the five experts on DOD-Obstructive was 84.3%, with a median kappa of 76.5%.
source: The median accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring of the five experts was 84.3%, with a median kappa of 76.5%.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: YASA was not significantly different from the Stephansen et al., 2018 algorithm or human scorers 1, 3, 4, and 5 on DOD-Obstructive.
source: Pairwise comparisons of accuracy showed that YASA was not significantly different from the Stephansen et al., 2018 algorithm or human scorers 1, 3, 4, and 5.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: Human scorer 2 had a significantly lower accuracy than YASA on DOD-Obstructive (p=0.004).
source: Human scorer 2 had a significantly lower accuracy (p=0.004), while the Perslev algorithm had a significantly higher accuracy (p=0.009).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: The Perslev algorithm had a significantly higher accuracy than YASA on DOD-Obstructive (p=0.009).
source: Human scorer 2 had a significantly lower accuracy (p=0.004), while the Perslev algorithm had a significantly higher accuracy (p=0.009).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: YASA outperformed the Stephansen et al., 2018 algorithm and four out of five scorers for N3 sleep on DOD-Obstructive (all p's<0.01).
source: Pairwise comparisons of F1-scores showed that YASA outperformed the Stephansen et al., 2018 algorithm and four out of five scorers for N3 sleep (all p's<0.01).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: The Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm had significantly higher scores than YASA for N1, REM and wakefulness on DOD-Obstructive (all p's<0.011).
source: However, the Perslev et al., 2021 algorithm had significantly higher scores than YASA for N1, REM and wakefulness (all p's<0.011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: The accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring was significantly higher during stable epochs compared to transition epochs on the combined DOD dataset (mean ± STD: 91.2 ± 7.8 vs. 68.95 ± 7.7, p<0.001).
source: Additional analyses on the combined dataset (n = 75 nights, healthy and patients combined) revealed that, first, the accuracy of YASA against the consensus scoring was significantly higher during stable epochs compared to transition epochs (mean ± STD: 91.2 ± 7.8 vs. 68.95 ± 7.7, p<0.001), or in epochs that were marked as high confidence by the algorithm (93.9 ± 6.0 vs. 64.1 ± 7.0 for low-confidence epochs, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: Epochs with unanimous consensus from the five human experts were four times more likely to occur during stable epochs than transition epochs on the combined DOD dataset (46.2% ± 12.1% of all epochs vs. 11.5% ± 4.9%, p<0.001).
source: Second, epochs with unanimous consensus from the five human experts were four times more likely to occur during stable epochs than transition epochs (46.2% ± 12.1% of all epochs vs. 11.5% ± 4.9%, p<0.001) and also four times more likely to occur during epochs marked as high confidence (≥80%) by the algorithm (46.4% ± 12.9% of all epochs vs. 11.3% ± 5.7%, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the percentage of epochs marked as high confidence by YASA and the percent of epochs with unanimous consensus on the combined DOD dataset (r = 0.561, p<0.001).
source: Third, there was a significant correlation between the percentage of epochs marked as high confidence by YASA and the percent of epochs with unanimous consensus (r = 0.561, p<0.001), meaning that YASA was overall more confident in recordings with higher human interrater agreement.
evidence: This is directly stated in the validation results section.

claim: Age showed a small but significant negative correlation with accuracy (r = −0.128, p=0.002).
source: As with human sleep scoring, analyses focused on the first factor of age revealed a small but significant negative correlation with accuracy (r = −0.128, p=0.002, Figure 2A), suggesting a moderate linear decrease of accuracy with age.
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Body composition was not significantly correlated with accuracy (r = −0.001, p=0.97).
source: Second, body composition was not significantly correlated with accuracy (r = −0.001, p=0.97, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sex was not a significant determinant of accuracy (Welch's T = −1.635, p=0.103).
source: Third, sex was not a significant determinant of accuracy either (Welch's T = −1.635, p=0.103, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Sleep apnea (AHI) was negatively correlated with accuracy (r = −0.29, p<0.001).
source: Fourth, sleep apnea, and specifically the AHI, was negatively correlated with accuracy (r = −0.29, p<0.001, Figure 2E) as well as the overall confidence level of the algorithm (calculated by averaging the epoch-by-epoch confidence across the entire night, r = −0.339, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sleep apnea (AHI) was negatively correlated with the overall confidence level of the algorithm (r = −0.339, p<0.001).
source: Fourth, sleep apnea, and specifically the AHI, was negatively correlated with accuracy (r = −0.29, p<0.001, Figure 2E) as well as the overall confidence level of the algorithm (calculated by averaging the epoch-by-epoch confidence across the entire night, r = −0.339, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section.

claim: The percentage of (human-defined) stage transitions was significantly correlated with the AHI (r = 0.427, p<0.001).
source: Consistent with the latter, the percentage of (human-defined) stage transitions was significantly correlated with the AHI (r = 0.427, p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section.

claim: Race was a significant predictor of accuracy (ANOVA, F(3, 581) = 3.281, p=0.021).
source: Finally, race was a significant predictor of accuracy (ANOVA, F(3, 581) = 3.281, p=0.021, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Accuracy was lower in Hispanic than in non-Hispanic White individuals (p=0.032).
source: Pairwise post hoc tests adjusted for multiple comparisons with Tukey's method revealed that accuracy was lower in Hispanic than in non-Hispanic White individuals (p=0.032).
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section.

claim: The percentage of N1 sleep and percentage of stage transitions were the two top predictors of accuracy, accounting for 40% of the total relative importance.
source: The percentage of N1 sleep and percentage of stage transitions – both markers of sleep fragmentation – were the two top predictors of accuracy, accounting for 40% of the total relative importance.
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Supplementary file 3b.

claim: The combined contribution of age, sex, race, and medical diagnosis of insomnia, hypertension, diabetes, and depression accounted for roughly 10% of the total importance in predicting accuracy.
source: By contrast, the combined contribution of age, sex, race, and medical diagnosis of insomnia, hypertension, diabetes, and depression accounted for roughly 10% of the total importance.
evidence: This is directly stated in the moderator analyses section and shown in Supplementary file 3b.

claim: 11 out of the top 20 features are derived from the electroencephalogram (EEG) signal.
